About me


Ever since my introductory microbiology course, I knew I wanted to study microbial ecology and the ecosystemic functions that microbial and viral communities realize. Our world is in dire need of understanding and appreciating differences, and within that struggle, it’s our responsibility as eukaryotes to recognize the irreplaceable tasks that prokaryotes, archaea and viruses have realized for millions of years in order to produce resilient ecosystems that now face exponentially compounding adversity day after day.



Sampling the northern coast, Isabela, P.R.

I’m currently working in the ViDaB Lab at UPRM studying cyanophage diversity throughout the Puerto Rican archipelago. I look at how viral abundance fluctuates throughout the 12 months of the year in addition to studying the genetic diversity across different aquatic ecosystems. Viruses are crucial drivers of genetic mobility, regulators of nutrient cycling, and vital stabilizers of algae blooms, which are commonly derived from anthropogenic interference and nutrient runoff. With this research, I hope to better understand the Puerto Rican ecosystem and its vital aquatic systems from a microbial perspective, helping to build a more resilient ecology in the future.
